newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan shuffles cabinet in anti-crime strategy.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan shuffles cabinet in anti-crime strategy.

text.p: Taiwan's ruling Nationalist Party approved a modest reshuffle of the beleaguered cabinet on Wednesday, hoping an injection of fresh talent would ease public anger over a perceived breakdown of law and order.

There were no surprises in the list of six appointments, announced by party secretary general Wu Po-hsiung after a party central standing committee meeting. It conformed with a draft roster leaked to local media on Sunday.
As expected, Premier Lien Chan ignored opposition calls for his own resignation. Lien has pledged to resign in July.
Wu told reporters the partial reshuffle was President Lee Teng-hui's response to the public uproar over lawlessness.
"Chairman Lee is concerned about the latest developments in society and feels the need to have a partial reshuffle," Wu said, referring to Lee by his title of party chairman.
The shakeup and Lien's vow to step down soon appeared to appease some of the cabinet's fiercer critics, but pressure on the government was likely to continue.

Lee faces tough questioning at an annual news conference on Thursday and opposition lawmakers plan to raise a non-binding motion in parliament on Friday demanding Lien's ouster -- the third such move in less than two weeks.
Another test of the reshuffle's success will come on Sunday when civic leaders have called for a mass march against crime.
The last such protest on May 4 drew 50,000 people.

The most significant cabinet portfolio -- interior minister -- was handed to Yeh Ching-feng, who was in the cabinet without a portfolio and becomes the first woman to head the interior ministry, which oversees Taiwan's police.

Incumbent Lin Feng-cheng, who resigned on May 8, had come under fire over a wave of serious and still unsolved crimes that have swept the island in recent months -- most recently the kidnap and murder of a television celebrity's teenage daughter.
Taiwan was stunned again on Tuesday by police revelations that a 15-year-old boy was kidnapped and killed just two days after media reported the abduction of 17-year-old Pai Hsiao-yen.
The unrelated cases, in which both victims were snatched on their way to school, touched a raw nerve in Taiwan, where public anger has been simmering over a number of sensational crimes.

Police have yet to crack the gangland-style execution in November 1996 of northern Taoyuan county's magistrate and seven others in his home. Nine people were methodically bound and shot in the head at point-blank range. Only one survived.
Also unsolved is the murder of a feminist opposition politician who was found dead of 35 stab wounds in southern Kaohsiung two weeks after the Taoyuan killings.
Another important cabinet portfolio, that of government spokesman, went to David Lee, a career diplomat who recently served as deputy chief of the Government Information Office.
Lee replaces information office chief Su Chi, who was promoted to minister without portfolio.
A conspicuous hole in the cabinet, created by the surprise resignation of Nationalist Party "golden boy" Ma Ying-jeou, was filled by Chao Shou-po, the cabinet's secretary general.
Ma, who had been justice minister until mid-1996 and more recently a minister without portfolio, said he quit to take responsibility for the cabinet's poor record against crime.
His resignation cast doubt on party plans to run the charismatic Ma in future elections. His replacement ended speculation that Lien and Lee would reject his resignation.

Peng Tso-kuei was named to replace Council of Agriculture chairman Tjiu Mau-ying, who resigned to take responsibility for a hog foot and mouth disease epidemic that has brought billions of dollars of losses to Taiwan's feed lots since March 20.
Hsu Chieh-kwei was named to head the cabinet's Council of Labour, replacing Hsieh Sheng-shan, who quit to stand in the election for magistrate of Taipei county.
